claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 exists as a single BCC phase at the stated high-temperature starting condition.
Al addition thermodynamically stabilizes the BCC lattice.
In Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 at high temperature, Al lowers the free energy of BCC relative to FCC and intermetallic phases.
Diffusion is intrinsically sluggish in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
Slow diffusion kinetically hinders the atomic rearrangements required for transformation during cooling.
Phase stability in this alloy is governed by competition between Al-dependent BCC thermodynamic stabilization and kinetic arrest caused by slow diffusion.
The controlled comparison is an isothermal hold near a predicted transformation threshold versus rapid quenching from the high-temperature BCC state.
The control and annealed samples are prepared from the same homogenized alloy under inert or vacuum conditions.
A transformation-relevant temperature for this exact alloy can be selected using CALPHAD predictions.
Rapid quenching inhibits diffusional rearrangement, local chemical ordering, and redistribution of Al and other elements.
A prolonged isothermal hold permits diffusional rearrangement and local chemical ordering that can drive phase transformation.
An isothermal anneal near the transformation threshold can overcome enough of the kinetic barrier to destabilize BCC and promote transformation.
Rapid quenching will retain the high-temperature BCC phase at room temperature.
The isothermally held sample will exhibit a measurable reduction in BCC phase fraction.
The reduced BCC fraction will be accompanied by the appearance of FCC or minor secondary phases.
Phase-fraction and microstructural changes will be assessed using X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy.
Prior thermodynamic calculations support a qualitative association between higher Al content and increased BCC phase fraction in compositionally complex alloys.
The cited prior evidence supports sluggish transformation kinetics in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
No significant phase-fraction difference after an isothermal hold with ample time for diffusion would falsify the proposed thermodynamic-versus-kinetic explanation.
